subject: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
parts:
The right way to do all of these general calls seems
to be with the C++ notion of a callable object, or
functor. This'll be true not just for the finite diffs
stuff, but also for operations like optimization.

The signature for gradient by finite diffs would be
something like:

template <typename Scalar, typename Function>
S
grad_finite_diffs(const std::vector<Scalar>& x,
Function& f,
std::vector<S>& grad);

The return is the value of the function f at x.

Functor f must be callable as follows:

Scalar f(std::vector<Scalar>& x);

This generalizes the notion of a function pointer and
is the standard lib way to write general "algorithms"
like this in C++11. If f is a class or struct, it'll
just implement

Scalar operator()(std::vector<Scalar>& x);

and we're good to go (but see below for complications
due to int params in log_prob_grad).

The Scalar instances x[n] must implement
difference (Scalar - Scalar) and (Scalar + double),
the two ops involved in finite diffs.

We could limit the function to be stateless by
declaring it const.

The old C-style way of doing this would've been to
use a function pointer.

Now, in order for our prob_grad objects to play nicely,
we're going to need to use some fancy binding for the
int parameters. One way to do this would be to add
a functor factory:

typedef double functor_t(const std::vector<double>& x);

functor_t get_prob_functor(const std::vector<int>& params_i);

This seems a bit complex for users, so we could actually
skip the base class prob and implement prob_grad with
finite diffs based on plain old log_prob right in the base
prob_grad class. This'd then look just like what Matt did,
only it'd actually implement the gradient function.

double log_prob_grad_finite_diffs(
const std::vector<int>& params_i,
const std::vector<double>& params_r,
std::vector<double>& gradient);

Now we could just leave this in the base class prob_grad,
or noting that this is the same signature as the
pure virtual log_prob_grad() function, we could actually
implement it with this instead.

The clunkiness there is that you need to explicitly call
the parent class's implementation to get finite diffs
from an instance of log_prob_grad_ad.

Any preferences for how this goes?

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
parts:
On Feb 4, 2:04 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> The right way to do all of these general calls seems
> to be with the C++ notion of a callable object, or
> functor.  This'll be true not just for the finite diffs
> stuff, but also for operations like optimization.

For: Functors
Against: Anything resembling old C style

Also, I would definitely be for supporting Vectors in the Eigen sense
in addition to (or maybe to the exclusion of) Vectors in the std
sense.

There is a good example of using functors with Eigen in the nonlinear
optimization module of Eigen/unsupported.

Is there a purpose for finite-diff besides checking auto-dif? Either
way, I would also nominate "complex step" approximations, which are
considered better than finite-diff primarily because finite-diff is
prone to cancellation. Both involve adding a tiny h to the parameter,
but with complex step h is on the imaginary axis. The imaginary part
of the function output divided by h is a good approximation to the
partial derivative. Google [derivative "complex step"] for more info,
particularly anything written by Nick Higham in a matrix function
context. This should be really easy in Eigen with templated parameters
because Eigen already supports mixed operations between doubles and
complex doubles. Clearly, the downside is that this is limited to
functions that do sensible things with complex numbers.

Ben

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
parts:
I'll tentatively vote for a functor factory method in prob_grad, since it'll be useful for multiple things. That said, I still think it's valuable to have a function that just makes sure your gradients are correct. This is not just for checking auto-diff, but also for users (like me) who want to eliminate the overhead of auto-diff by writing their own gradient implementations. (Although this could also be accomplished, with higher precision, by a function that compared the auto-diff-based base implementation of grad_log_prob() with the possibly handwritten top-level implementation of grad_log_prob().)

Most of our functions don't do sensible things with complex numbers. Which I'm pretty comfortable with. It would, however, definitely be better to use the two-sided method of finite differences rather than the one-sided version I've got in there currently. (It's twice as expensive, but you don't use finite differences because it's fast.)

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
parts:
Glad we can agree on functors. We can
template out

std vectors: std::vector<T>
Eigen column vectors: Eigen<T,Dynamic,1>
Eigen row vectors: Eigen<T,1,Dynamic>
Eigen matrices: Eigen<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>

because they all support size() and unary [] (for
matrices, size is M x N and access is column-major
by default).

Matt previously suggested that we also support
plain old (T*,size_t). We could certainly implement
the Eigen and std::vector versions on (T*,size_t)
because they have size() and T* is just the start
iterator. Also, instead of size_t, we can also allow
the end iterator.

fun(T* ts, size_t length)

fun(iterator<T>* start, iterator<T>* end)

fun(std::vector<T>& ts);

fun(Matrix<T,M,N>& m); // templating M&N supports all versions

I'm not sure what the cleanest most idiomatic
thing is to do here. I'd like to support more than
Eigen types here. Eigen<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>
has a big advantage is speed and size over
std::vector<std::vector<T> >, because the former
uses one block of contiguous memory and the latter is
a bunch of std::vector<T>, each of which has its own
size.

Ben mentioned that Eigen [] checks the range, whereas
() doesn't, so we might even want to override for
more efficiency (depends on whether we want the checks
or not).

Looks like the Eigen developers are looking for
volunteers to write an optimization module:

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/index.php?title=Todo#Optimization_module

Do you know where I could find their finite
diff implementation?

I'm trying to be conservative on dependencies.
Right now, we only depend on the supported bits of
Eigen and Boost as dependencies.

I didn't bring in the unsupported modules from
Eigen or the RNG lib Ben menitoned yet, but we can
always add more dependencies.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: functors for finite diffs, optimization, etc.
parts:
Sorry for the confusing terminology. To put
it in proper C++ lingo, functors are just
objects that implement the function-call
operator() and hence can be called like functions.
C++11 lambda expressions give you a way of
creating anonymous functor-like objects that
can be called like functions.

To define a square root callable (as opposed
to function pointer), we could use an explicitly
named functor

struct sqrt_functor
double operator()(double x) { return sqrt(x); }
};

double y = sqrt_functor(2.0);

or a C++ lambda expression:

[](double x) { return sqrt(x); }

You can really think of [] as an anonymous way or
writing the functor's operator definition -- they use
the same definition starting at the argument
declaration (double x) (the lambda's return type is
automatically computed by the type of the return expression,
so it doesn't get declared; thankfully they've added
an "auto" super type inference type to make dealing with
this issue).

As a simple example, we could pass either the functor
or lambda expression to a function templated on
the callable F:

template <typename F, typename X>
double apply(F f, X x) {
return f(x);
}

Now the following four expressions all return
the square root of 2:

directly apply functor:

sqrt_functor()(2.0);

directly apply lambda expression:

([](double x) { return sqrt(x); })(2.0);

indirectly apply functor:

apply(sqrt_functor(),2.0);

indirectly apply lambda expression:

apply([](double x) { return sqrt(x); }, 2.0);

Acting like a function is an instance of what
C++ calls a "concept" -- it's the set of operations
and contexts an argument needs to be usable in to
instantiate a template.

So a finite differences method could be declared
using a templated callable and scalar as:

template <typename F, typename S>
S finite_diffs(F f, std::vector<S> x);

Though it's now more idiomatic to not call this kind
of thing with a vector, but with an iterator, but that
seems clunky in the context of multiple-argument functions.

The nice part of lambda expressions and functors is
that they have proper modern C++ behavior in that
they have proper value semantics, so they can be used
straightforwardly (and efficiently) without a whole
lot of reference/dereference hoo-ha. Stan's agrad::var
is another instance of something designed to have
proper value semantics. For simple functors like sqrt_functor,
it's even better in that the struct has no data, so it
can be treated by an optimizing compiler like a type and
no data need be passed anywhere.

Boost already provides a lot of lambda-like functionality
that I'm using for the parser to support lazy evaluation
(check out Boost's Phoenix library, which generalizes
Boost Lambda, which generalizes Boost Bind, which
generalizes pre C++99's built-in bind). Any of these
could also be used to define an appropriate callable.

Sorry -- that took a lot of explaining.

Back to our regularly scheduled programming.

- Bob
